stances.claim: Objections arose from the past -- some vague, some petty, some resurrected from decades-old client dissatisfaction; a former case was reexamined; an old grievance was amplified; others were deemed 'more qualified,' usually because they had climbed the judicial hierarchy instead of practicing law.

Art was not naïve -- he understood institutional caution; but the cumulative effect was corrosive -- each screening became a public exposure, each delay a whisper of doubt, each rejection a silent question: 'Was this calling real -- or self-invented?'

one_paragraph_summary: Art's seven-rejections chapter, opening with the framing that by the early 1990s he 'had done everything one was supposed to do before entering public service': professional independence, children raised into academic excellence, civic leadership without scandal, faith deepened into discipline. Yet 'when the call to serve finally came, it did not come gently -- it came with rejection.' From 1992 to 1995, vacancies opened repeatedly in the Supreme Court -- 'each time, Art's name was submitted to the Judicial and Bar Council; each time, it was scrutinized; each time, it was questioned; and each time, it was passed over.' Seven times. Objections were 'some vague, some petty, some resurrected from decades-old client dissatisfaction'; others were deemed 'more qualified,' usually because they had climbed the judicial hierarchy instead of practicing law. The cumulative effect was 'corrosive' -- each screening a public exposure, each delay a whisper of doubt, each rejection a silent question: 'Was this calling real -- or self-invented?' At night he prayed with increasing urgency: 'How long, O Lord?' 'Why humiliation if the path is Yours?' 'Why surrender ambition only to be tested again?' 'The law had taught him patience. Faith demanded more.' In January 1995, after the seventh rejection, 'something broke -- and something else was born.' He surrendered completely, praying 'not for appointment, but for removal of desire': 'Take all that I am. My career. My ambition. My will. Do what You want.' For the first time in years, he stopped hoping.
